did_you_know.text: The word boshes here means “was delayed” or “was late,” not “was ashamed.” Although it resembles the root meaning shame, its meaning in this verse is prolonged waiting.
The Hebrew word nezem can refer to jewelry worn in the ear or nose; here the verse specifies earrings. In the ancient world, such jewelry also served as a portable form of valuable property.
Egel masekhah does not mean “a calf wearing a mask.” The word masekhah is related to casting metal, so the phrase means a cast-metal calf.

The word letzachek can mean laughing or playing, but in this context it suggests behavior wilder than ordinary happiness. Many biblical words have a broader range of meaning than their usual modern translations.
The phrase “stiff-necked” is an image of an animal resisting a yoke and refusing to turn its neck. It came to describe someone stubborn and unwilling to accept guidance.
The verb vayechal means “pleaded” or “begged for mercy.” Moses is not merely reporting facts; he is actively intervening to defend the people.
“Israel” in this verse is another name for Jacob, not only the name of the nation. Moses invokes the three patriarchs to base his appeal on earlier covenant promises.
The Sages later connected the word charut, “engraved,” with cherut, “freedom.” This wordplay links the Torah with spiritual freedom.

According to rabbinic tradition, the broken tablets were not discarded; they were placed in the Ark beside the whole tablets. The fragments thus became a symbol that failure does not erase the value of what came before.
Aaron’s answer sounds like an excuse: he describes throwing the gold into the fire but leaves out the shaping of the statue. In this way, his wording minimizes his responsibility.
The phrase mil’u yedkhem is a biblical idiom meaning “dedicate yourselves to a role or service.” It also appears in descriptions of the priests’ ordination.
Moses’ request, “Please erase me from Your book,” expresses his willingness to share the people’s fate. His leadership is presented as personal responsibility, not merely giving orders.
